assessment.summary: KRAS is one of the most extensively studied oncology targets, with 556 high-resolution PDB structures (best at 0.953Å), two FDA-approved covalent inhibitors (sotorasib and adagrasib targeting G12C), and nearly 6,000 ChEMBL IC50 entries. Druggability is high for the G12C mutant specifically, though broader mutant coverage (G12D, G12V, G13D, etc.) and wild-type selectivity remain active challenges. The target is exceptionally well-validated across multiple cancer indications.
evidence_gaps: Approved drugs (sotorasib, adagrasib) are selective for G12C mutation only; druggability of other common KRAS mutations (G12D, G12V, G12R, G13D) is less established clinically
Median IC50 of ~1020 nM suggests many ChEMBL compounds have modest potency, indicating chemical space for non-covalent inhibitors is still maturing
Resistance mechanisms (e.g., secondary KRAS mutations, bypass signalling via RTKs, MAPK reactivation) limit durable clinical efficacy and are not fully addressed
Wild-type KRAS selectivity window for non-covalent inhibitors is not well characterised, raising potential toxicity concerns
Allele-specific structural differences for non-G12C mutants may require distinct chemical strategies not yet reflected in approved agents
PPI (protein-protein interaction) inhibition of KRAS-effector interfaces (e.g., RAF, PI3K) remains largely undrugged despite structural data
